The patient presents with acute confusional state and progressive lethargy — classic neurologic manifestations of severe, acute-on-chronic hyponatremia. The serum sodium of 122 mEq/L is life-threatening and explains the encephalopathy. Critically, serum glucose is normal (105 mg/dL), confirming *true* (non-pseudohyponatremic) hyponatremia. Urine studies show inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osmolality 334 mOsm/kg > serum osmolality — inferred as low given profound hyponatremia) and significant urinary sodium excretion (45 mEq/L), which — in the absence of hypovolemia or diuretic use — strongly indicates inappropriate ADH secretion. Among euvolemic causes, SIADH is by far the most common, especially in acute confusional states without obvious alternative etiology (e.g., no documented malignancy, pulmonary infection, or CNS trauma yet — but these remain to be ruled out). While adrenal insufficiency and myxedema coma can cause euvolemic hyponatremia, they are far less common than SIADH and would typically present with additional features (e.g., hypotension, hyperpigmentation, bradycardia, hypothermia, or markedly elevated TSH/cortisol deficiency) — none of which are reported. The absence of documented volume depletion or overload, combined with high urine osmolality and urine Na⁺, makes hypovolemic (e.g., vomiting/diarrhea) or hypervolemic (e.g., HF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome) causes highly unlikely. - Profound true hyponatremia (Na⁺ = 122 mEq/L) with normal serum glucose → confirms symptomatic hypoosmolar hyponatremia.

Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion (SIADH)
